title: What staff training does the Banking Code of Practice require?
seoTitle: Banking Code of Practice staff training
description: The training commitments in the 2025 Banking Code of Practice, paragraph by paragraph, how the BCCC monitors them, and the 2026 Banking Code review timetable.
shortAnswer: The 2025 Banking Code of Practice, published by the Australian Banking Association (ABA) and approved by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), took effect on February 28, 2025. Paragraph 7 commits subscribing banks to train staff and representatives so they can work competently, understand and comply with the Code, and treat vulnerable customers with sensitivity, respect and compassion. Further paragraphs require cultural awareness training and training to recognize customers eligible for low or no fee accounts.
keyTakeaways: The current edition was published on June 27, 2024 and has been effective since February 28, 2025; an independent review of the Code began on September 4, 2026.

Paragraph 7 is the general training commitment and covers both staff and representatives, with three required outcomes: competence, Code compliance, and respectful treatment of diverse and vulnerable customers.
Paragraphs 49 and 50 require cultural awareness training for staff who regularly assist Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander customers and guarantors, and make it available to all other staff.

Paragraph 66 requires training to help staff recognize people who may qualify for a basic, low or no fee account, and paragraph 11 requires advice to come from staff who are authorized and trained to give it.
The Banking Code Compliance Committee (BCCC) monitors compliance under its Charter, and paragraph 6 binds banks to that Charter.
jurisdiction: Australia (national industry code approved by ASIC)
regulator: Banking Code Compliance Committee (BCCC); Code approved by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC)
appliesTo: Banks that subscribe to the Banking Code of Practice
Bank staff and representatives who provide banking services to individuals, small businesses and guarantors
Frontline, lending, collections, deceased estates and complaints teams
Staff who regularly assist Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander customers and guarantors

sections.heading: Which edition of the Banking Code applies?

blocks.text: The 2025 edition of the [Banking Code of Practice](https://www.ausbanking.org.au/banking-code/) is the current version: its cover states a published date of June 27, 2024 and an effective date of February 28, 2025. ASIC announced its approval in [media release 24-136MR](https://www.asic.gov.au/about-asic/news-centre/find-a-media-release/2024-releases/24-136mr-asic-approves-enhanced-banking-code-of-practice), describing enhancements that include improved inclusivity and accessibility, new deceased estates provisions, a broader financial difficulty definition, and stronger guarantor protections.

The Code covers individuals, small businesses and guarantors. The 2025 definition treats a business as a small business if it had annual turnover under $10 million in the previous financial year, has fewer than 100 full time equivalent employees, and has less than $5 million total debt to all credit providers. ASIC notes that the borrowing threshold rose from $3 million to $5 million. That matters for training scope: business bankers who deal with clients under those thresholds are delivering Code services.

blocks.title: Currency and review
blocks.text: This page reflects the 2025 Banking Code of Practice as at November 2026. An independent [2026 Banking Code Review](https://www.2026bankingcodereview.com.au/) led by Peter Kell began on September 4, 2026. Written submissions close on December 11, 2026, an interim report is planned for March 2027, and the final report is due to the ABA by June 30, 2027. Paragraph numbers may change in a later edition.

Paragraph 7, headed "Trained and competent staff", is the Code's general training commitment. It reads: "We will make sure that our staff and our representatives are trained so that they: a) can competently do their work; b) understand the Code and how to comply with it when they are providing Banking Services to you; and c) treat our diverse customers, vulnerable customers and customers who appear to be vulnerable with sensitivity, respect and compassion."

Three design points follow from the wording. First, "representatives" brings third parties acting for the bank into scope, so contracts with brokers or outsourced service providers need a training clause. Second, limb (b) ties training to the Code itself, not only to internal procedure, which means staff should be able to explain the Code commitments relevant to their role. Third, limb (c) extends to customers who "appear to be vulnerable", so training has to build the skill of noticing, not only of responding once a customer discloses.

Paragraph 5 sits beside it: banks will do all things necessary to provide banking services "efficiently, honestly and fairly", which the Code says is the same standard as section 912A(1)(a) of the Corporations Act 2001 and section 47(1)(a) of the National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009. Paragraph 11 adds that advice on banking services will come through staff who are authorized and trained to give it.

sections.heading: Which other paragraphs name specific training?

blocks.text: Three further paragraphs name a training activity outright, and several more describe capabilities that in practice can only be delivered through role specific training. The table separates the two so that a training plan can show which items are express Code commitments and which are inferred capabilities.

blocks.text: Paragraph 50 is easy to misread. It requires cultural awareness training to be made available to all staff, not completed by all staff, while paragraph 49 requires it to be provided to those who regularly assist Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander customers. A [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix) should therefore mark the course as required for defined roles and optional for everyone else.

sections.heading: How do Code commitments map to roles, frequency and evidence?

blocks.text: The Code does not set training intervals or prescribe record formats, so the bank has to choose and justify them. The table below is an original, illustrative mapping. The frequencies are design choices for a bank to adapt, not Code requirements, and the evidence column reflects what a BCCC inquiry or an internal audit would reasonably ask for.

blocks.text: The guide to [setting mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) explains how to document the rationale for intervals like these, and [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations) covers building the paragraph to role links.

sections.heading: How does the BCCC monitor training commitments?

blocks.text: The BCCC is the independent body that monitors banks' compliance with the Code, and its powers, including sanctions, are set out in the BCCC Charter rather than in the Code. Paragraph 6 states that banks are "bound by our obligations in the BCCC Charter", and the Code's introduction commits banks to co-operate and comply with all reasonable requests of the BCCC in its monitoring and investigative activities.

The introduction also explains that the BCCC collects information about potential breaches, "particularly issues that may be serious or systemic in nature", and is not a complaints resolution body; individual complaints go to the bank's internal dispute resolution process and then the Australian Financial Complaints Authority. For training, the practical consequence is that a systemic failure, such as staff consistently missing vulnerability indicators, is the kind of issue the BCCC investigates, and the bank will need to show what training was given, to whom, and how competence was checked. The guide to [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) sets out a record structure that answers those questions.

ASIC's release on the 2025 Code says its rules are binding on ABA members and form part of the contracts between banks and their customers. Training failures can therefore surface in customer disputes as well as in BCCC monitoring.

sections.heading: How does the Code interact with other training obligations?

blocks.text: The Code adds to, and does not replace, legal obligations: paragraph 4 says that where the Code imposes an obligation additional to the law, the bank will comply with the Code unless that would breach the law or relevant regulatory obligation or guidance. A bank's Code training therefore sits inside a wider program that includes AML/CTF training under the [AUSTRAC requirements](/regulations/austrac-aml-ctf-training-requirements), product governance training under the [design and distribution obligations](/regulations/design-and-distribution-obligations-staff-training), and operational risk capability under [APRA CPS 230](/regulations/apra-cps-230-operational-risk-training).

Overlaps are worth designing for. Vulnerability recognition, for example, supports paragraph 7(c), the efficiently, honestly and fairly standard restated in paragraph 5, and product distribution decisions. A single, well assessed vulnerability module mapped to all three is easier to defend than three separate courses with inconsistent content. More context on the sector is on the [financial services industry page](/industries/financial-services).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models the Code paragraphs, the roles they apply to and the capabilities they imply as a structured framework before any content is written. When the 2026 review produces a new edition, changed paragraphs can be traced to the affected roles and assessments, and each staff record shows which Code version the person was assessed against.

faqs.q: Does the Banking Code require annual training?
faqs.a: No. The 2025 Code requires staff and representatives to be trained to the outcomes in paragraph 7 and names specific training in paragraphs 49, 50 and 66, but it does not set a refresh interval. Banks set and justify their own frequency, typically at induction, after Code changes and on a periodic cycle.

faqs.q: Do brokers and other third parties need Banking Code training?
faqs.a: Paragraph 7 covers "our staff and our representatives", so people acting for the bank in providing banking services fall within the commitment. Banks usually address this through contract terms requiring training against the relevant Code commitments and through periodic assurance over the third party's records.

faqs.q: Is the Banking Code legally enforceable?
faqs.a: ASIC states that the Code's rules are binding on ABA members and form part of the contracts between banks and their customers. Compliance is monitored by the Banking Code Compliance Committee under its Charter, which banks are bound by under paragraph 6 of the Code.

faqs.q: Will the training commitments change after the 2026 review?
faqs.a: Possibly. The independent review led by Peter Kell commenced on September 4, 2026 and its final report is due by June 30, 2027, with the ABA's response due by December 11, 2027. Any new edition would need ASIC approval before it replaced the 2025 Code.
